title: ICPC 2025
markdown:
# ICPC 2025

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

First competitive programming contest. Went in not really knowing what to expect.

I took the easier end of the problem set — solved Snakey String and Memories of Passport Control, which let my teammates focus on harder stuff without having to come back and clean up. That part of the strategy worked. What didn't was problem queue management — nobody was tracking how long we'd been on something, and toward the end we had overlap and wasted time we could've spent elsewhere.

Spent the back half of the contest stuck on "Much Room for Mushrooms." Had the right shape of the solution — something involving even/odd parity and combinatorial counting — but couldn't turn the intuition into actual math. The logic was there. The formulas weren't. Ended up spinning.

## Where the gaps are

Combinatorics, closed-form derivation, parity tricks. I can reason through problems but I don't have the standard formulas memorized, so I'm re-deriving from scratch under time pressure. Also need to practice standard algorithms (DP, graph traversal) until implementation is automatic, not something I have to figure out mid-contest.

Next time someone needs to own the queue and call time when a problem has stalled long enough.

title: JMU Makeathon, Fall 2026
markdown:
# JMU Makeathon, Fall 2026

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

We built Echoes: anonymous voice notes pinned to real places on campus. You can only hear or record one by standing at the spot. Popular ones become Legends, and some point to real clubs and events.

We placed third. We went in expecting first, because we had a full working demo that everyone in the room could open on their phone and use at the same time. We still came third.

## What we did

The prompt gave us a problem that is easy to say badly. Nobody can break your comfort zone for you, so we did not promise friendships. Our pitch was "you help us help you": the student takes the step, and the app makes that step smaller. To hear an echo you have to go somewhere. To post one you only have to talk, anonymously. Replies and "open doors" point at clubs and events that already exist.

I came up with the idea and wrote the outline. David and I ran most of the presentation and coordination and decided what needed to be built. Luke built almost all of the demo (a Go backend and a React frontend with a satellite map). Curtis helped us shape the idea and the presentation. The research changed how we pitched it. The core mechanic, geo-locked audio, already exists in other apps, and two of them are even called Echoes. So the outline names them and says what is different: Legends, open doors, warm replies, and guardrails learned from Yik Yak.

## What I learned

**The idea was about 90% of the work.** Once we had it, getting the app running and the presentation built was the rest. That split is fine, but it means the idea has to be settled early and be good enough to carry everything else.

**Put the effort into the demo, not the backend.** People remember the demo. It needs to be simple, make sense, work, and prove the idea does what we say. A complex backend or anything very technical does not need to exist. It can be explained. Next time we spend more time polishing the demo and the presentation and less on a fleshed-out app.

**Get the whole idea across.** This is the problem I had in the last two hackathons, and I think it is the most important one. The pitch should make sure the judges understand the full idea before it spends time on marketing and business details. We had those details ready, and they are the part to cut first.

I don't know exactly why we were third, and I have no judge feedback. My guesses: geo-locked audio is not new, we had no proof it helps, and our answers on moderation and an empty map at launch were plans and not things we had tested. A working demo that everyone could use at once did not win it alone.

title: JMU Blue Team Mock Competition
markdown:
# JMU Blue Team Mock Competition

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

First internal competition the club has run. The format was exactly what you'd want for actually learning something: attackers who explain what they did and why it worked.

I took Windows because nobody else was doing it and it seemed like a gap worth filling. Also, after regionals I wanted to own a host instead of just a firewall.

Started by doing what every Windows hardening guide says — changed the admin password, turned on Windows Defender, enabled audit logging. Felt good about it for about 15 minutes. The attacker got in through a misconfigured IIS app pool I hadn't touched, found credentials in a batch script I hadn't noticed, and leveraged an unpatched service from 2023. The password change did basically nothing.

The part that actually worked was staying curious when things went wrong. I asked the attackers why each exploit worked, not just what it did. That loop — attack, explain, fix, then attack again — accelerated learning more than any external competition I've been to. By the end of the session the box was meaningfully harder to crack. Not secure, but visibly better. Real iteration.

Real-time feedback from someone actively trying to break what you built is how you actually improve. Delayed scoreboard updates don't come close.

## Where I landed

Windows defense as a specialization going forward. Underrepresented in the club, common in enterprise environments, and it turned out to be genuinely interesting. Next semester I want to try the red team side of the same event — learn how to break what I'm building to defend.

title: JMUS Makeathon, Spring 2026
markdown:
# JMUS Makeathon, Spring 2026

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

We built Jarvis — an AI home automation system that learned your routines and managed your environment through natural language. Smart lights, thermostat, calendar integration, all running off a Raspberry Pi hub. The live demo was genuinely impressive.

We didn't place.

When we asked why, the feedback was: "We loved the presentation, but we're not entirely sure what the product is." We'd optimized so hard for emotional resonance — decision fatigue, better sleep, living instead of managing — that we forgot to clearly answer what it actually did or why it was better than Google Home. The story buried the product.

It's a weird failure mode. You can be too good at presentation and still lose because the audience doesn't understand what they saw.

I'd also floated a different idea mid-hackathon — Frontline, a missing persons locator using peer-to-peer mesh networking and Verizon's disaster-response towers to work offline during natural disasters. We passed on it because Jarvis was nearly done and Frontline would've been hard to finish cleanly. On the last day, another team presented almost exactly that concept and placed higher than us. Their version was less fleshed out than what I'd sketched, but they had a clearer pitch.

## Takeaway

Lead with clarity, add polish second. A mediocre presentation of a clear idea beats a beautiful presentation of a confusing one. Also: don't dismiss your B ideas just because your A idea is already done.

title: MACCDC 2026 Qualifiers
markdown:
# MACCDC 2026 Qualifiers

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

First defensive competition. I was on the firewall the whole time — Palo Alto NextGen managing the subnet gateway. That part went well: kept the rules clean, built a Red Team blocklist as IPs showed up, maintained rollback capability so I could harden aggressively without risking cascading failures. No self-inflicted downtime.

The thing that went wrong wasn't on my box. Our Splunk monitoring server got taken because nobody owned it. Nobody rotated the default credentials, nobody confirmed it was locked down. Red Team found it, changed the scoring heartbeat protocol from HTTP to HTTPS, and the automated scoring bot stopped reaching it. We lost major points from a box that was completely healthy underneath.

That's the lesson: unowned systems get exploited. In a competition, every box needs a named owner before the event starts, and credential rotation needs to happen in the first 30 minutes, not whenever someone gets around to it. A service owner matrix would've caught this.

Going into regionals, that's the main thing I want to fix: ownership assigned before we go live, and hardening treated like a checklist with a timer, not a free-form activity.

title: MACCDC 2026 Regionals
markdown:
# MACCDC 2026 Regionals

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

48 hours of live network defense. First time doing this in a serious competitive environment. Results were bad. Learning was good.

Services started failing early and I assumed it was the firewall. My role was firewall admin so naturally I blamed the firewall. I spent most of 30 hours writing, rewriting, and overwriting rules — each time convinced the next change would fix it. By hour 8 the ruleset was a mess of overlapping, conflicting policies.

On day 2 I finally did what I should have done on day 1: ran tcpdump and opened the capture in Wireshark. The problem was immediately obvious. Packets from the scoring server were looping back to themselves — a layer 2 network loop, two switches with no spanning tree configuration, packets bouncing infinitely. Nothing I was ever going to do with firewall rules would have fixed that.

That was hard to sit with. 30+ hours on a problem that had nothing to do with my job.

The root cause wasn't really technical. We showed up without understanding our own network. No topology diagram, no service inventory, no baseline to compare against. When things started breaking we had no reference for what "working" looked like. CTF mindset applied wrong — in CTFs you understand your target before you attack it. In blue team you understand your infrastructure before someone attacks it. If you don't, you're guessing from the start.

Also: when I'm a hammer, everything looks like a firewall rule. Should have escalated to someone checking layer 2 on day 1 instead of staying siloed for 30 hours.

## What changes next time

Preparation is the actual work. Network topology diagram a week out. Service inventory and ownership assigned before going live. Traffic baseline captured in a quiet moment. Always capture packets before touching rules.

title: RVASEC15
markdown:
# RVASEC15

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

Went planning to compete in the CTF. Left with something more useful.

Jake Kouns — security industry veteran, knew our club advisor — gave JMU tickets directly. That turned out to matter more than I expected going in. Walking in with an implicit voucher from someone people recognize meant professionals were actually willing to talk.

Day 1, I went to the first keynote just to orient myself and never came back to the CTF. A panel of CISOs and founders discussing the future of the field, and one of them said something like: "The best security person isn't the one who knows the most tools. It's the one who can communicate what they know to non-technical stakeholders." I closed my laptop.

Spent the rest of Day 1 in conversations. Threat intel analyst at a Fortune 500, security startup founder, a red team operator. Every single one came back to the same thing: technical skill is the entry ticket, communication is what differentiates you. Can you write the report? Can you explain this to a non-technical CEO? Do people want to work with you? The red teamer specifically: "Every red teamer can escalate privileges. What separates you is whether you can document it clearly and explain to a client why it matters."

Day 2 I solved 8 challenges in an hour (easy-medium range), hit something hard, gave up after 15 minutes, and went to talks instead. Booth crawl in the afternoon. Left with 4-5 emails from people who explicitly said reach out after graduation.

Wouldn't have gotten any of that grinding a laptop for 8 hours.

## The shift

Competitions train technical skills. Conferences train everything else. CTF practice is always available — it's online, unlimited, I can do it any day. I can attend RVASEC once a year. Optimize for what's rare.

Also: being good and people knowing you're good are different things. Planning to write more, document more, build something that exists outside of competition scoreboards.

title: Summit CTF 2026
markdown:
# Summit CTF 2026

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

48 hours. Probably the most educational event I've done so far, partly because the arc went wrong in an instructive way.

We came in with the upgraded automation framework from VMI and dominated the jeopardy portion early — had more flags than anyone else by hour 8. Teams from UVA, William & Mary, VCU all behind us on the scoreboard.

Then jeopardy dried up and we hit the live network. That's where automation stops helping and actual hands-on skill takes over. Privilege escalation, custom exploit chains, service enumeration under time pressure — we were slow at all of it. The scoreboard flipped as teams with real experience pulled ahead. We fell from first to mid-pack fast. It stung.

What pulled us back was just stubbornness. We started treating the live network like a documentation project — listing every service, every port, every failed attempt. Rotating shifts so someone was always fresh. A lot of the flags in a realistically-designed environment aren't in clever places, they're in predictable ones that only get found by being thorough. Found another 17+ flags over the next 36 hours through patient enumeration and following attacker logic.

9th place.

## The big lesson

All the information you need is online. The gap between teams isn't usually secret knowledge, it's how much they've practiced applying what's publicly available. The top teams had 2-3 deep specializations — UVA was strong on priv esc, William & Mary owned web exploitation. We were 6 people trying to cover 6 categories and were mediocre at all of them.

Depth beats breadth in competition. I need to pick something and go deep.

title: VMI CyberFusion 2026: CTF Orchestrator Overview
markdown:
# VMI CyberFusion 2026: CTF Orchestrator Overview

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

## Project Overview

This tool was engineered specifically for **VMI CyberFusion 26** to maximize efficiency and placement potential through automation. It functions as a hybrid **CTF Orchestrator** and **AI Solver**.

## Technical Architecture

### 1. The Core (Flask + Socket.IO)

The application is built on **Flask**, providing a lightweight yet extensible backend. **Socket.IO** is utilized for full-duplex communication, allowing the server to push real-time terminal logs, agent thoughts, and flag submissions to the frontend without polling.

### 2. The Runtime (Docker)

Security and consistency are paramount. The system leverages **Docker** to spawn ephemeral containers based on a custom `ctf-kali` image.
- **Isolation**: Malicious challenges or unstable exploits cannot harm the host.
- **Tooling**: The `ctf-kali:latest` image ensures all necessary binaries (nmap, gdb, pwntools) are pre-installed and available to the agent.

### 3. The Brain (OpenAI API)

The defining feature is the **OpenAI-powered agent**.
- **Context Awareness**: The agent consumes challenge descriptions and file metadata.
- **Action Loop**: It operates in a loop proposing a command, executing it in Docker, observing the output, and refining the strategy.
- **Autonomy**: Capable of solving standard categories (crypto, misc, basic pwn).

## Strategic Value

In a time-constrained environment like VMI CyberFusion, this tool provides:

- **Parallelism**: The agent can work on "easy" challenges while human operators focus on "hard" ones.
- **Expertise**: While many ctf competitions can be completed solo, teams are usually involved in order to cover topics more thoroughly. AI can fill in gaps for solo competitors so they can either improve on areas they don't know or straight solve them as a teammate.

## Deployment

The system is designed for "drop-in" usage:

1. Install dependencies:

   ```bash
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   ```

2. Add your API key to `config.json`.

3. Launch the server and open the dashboard at `http://localhost:7331`:

   ```bash
   python3 server.py
   ```

## Conclusion

This project demonstrates how modern DevOps practices and Generative AI can be applied to offensive security competitions, transforming the traditional solver into a force-multiplied command center.

title: VMI CyberFusion 2026 Retrospective
markdown:
# VMI CyberFusion 2026 Retrospective

[← All write-ups](../README.md)

## The Shift in Strategy

Reflecting on VMI CyberFusion 2026, the core takeaway wasn't about the individual challenges solved, but rather the methodology used to approach the competition. Instead of focusing grueling, manual effort on grinding through the CTF, the strategy pivoted towards building a platform to solve challenges in parallel.

Since artificial intelligence was inevitably going to be utilized during the competition, the goal became maximizing its efficiency. Rather than using AI as a simple chatbot for simple queries, the effort went into engineering a hybrid **CTF Orchestrator and AI Solver**.

## Why Build a Platform?

This approach fundamentally changed the experience of the competition:

- **Efficiency over Exhaustion:** The traditional approach to CTFs is grueling. By building an autonomous system, the competition became less of an endurance test and more of an exercise in command and control.
- **Parallel Problem Solving:** The platform enabled true parallelism. The OpenAI-powered agent could autonomously tackle standard categories (crypto, misc, basic pwn) by proposing commands, executing them in isolated Docker containers, and refining its strategy based on output. This freed up human operators to focus entirely on the complex, high-value challenges. These high-value challenges were also mostly solved by higher parameter yet more expensive models regardless.
- **Systematized AI:** Wrapping the AI in a robust architecture (a Flask/Socket.IO backend with Dockerized `ctf-kali` runtimes) turned a raw language model into a contextual, action-oriented agent.

## Conclusion

Ultimately, spending the time to develop this drop-in command center was a massive success. It transformed the competition from a series of isolated technical hurdles into a lesson in DevOps and offensive security automation. By accepting that AI is part of the modern CTF landscape and choosing to systematize it, the grueling nature of the competition was replaced with a highly efficient, force-multiplied approach.

Every CTF challenge was completed within 2 hours of its start, with 2 remaining hours to reflect and improve the platform further. Given more time and effort this platform can be utilized to complete more complex problems with higher token efficiency in the future.
